Management’s Discussion and Analysis (“MD&A”)

Quarterly Report on the Third Quarter of 2026

 

This portion of the Quarterly Report provides management’s discussion and analysis (“MD&A”) of the financial condition and results of operations, to enable a reader to assess material changes in financial condition and results of operations as at, and for the three and nine month period ended September 30, 2026, in comparison to the corresponding prior-year periods. The MD&A is intended to help the reader understand Barrick Mining Corporation (“Barrick”, “we”, “our”, the “Company” or the “Group”), our operations, financial performance as well as our present and future business environment. This MD&A, which has been prepared as of November 6, 2026, is intended to supplement and complement the condensed unaudited interim consolidated financial statements and notes thereto, prepared in accordance with IFRS Accounting Standards as issued by the International Accounting Standards Board applicable to the preparation of interim financial statements, under International Accounting Standard 34, Interim Financial Reporting, for the three and nine month period ended September 30, 2026 (collectively, the “Financial Statements”), which are included in this Quarterly Report on pages 60 to 64. You are encouraged to review the Financial Statements in conjunction with your review of this MD&A. This MD&A should be read in conjunction with both the

annual audited consolidated financial statements for the two years ended December 31, 2025, the related annual MD&A included in the 2025 Annual Report, and the most recent Form 40–F/Annual Information Form on file with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (“SEC”) and Canadian provincial securities regulatory authorities. These documents and additional information relating to the Company are available on SEDAR+ at www.sedarplus.ca and EDGAR at www.sec.gov. Certain notes to the Financial Statements are specifically referred to in this MD&A and such notes are incorporated by reference herein. All dollar amounts in this MD&A are in millions of United States dollars (“$” or “US$”), unless otherwise specified.

For the purposes of preparing our MD&A, we consider the materiality of information. Information is considered material if: (i) such information results in, or would reasonably be expected to result in, a significant change in the market price or value of our shares; (ii) there is a substantial likelihood that a reasonable investor would consider it important in making an investment decision; or (iii) it would significantly alter the total mix of information available to investors. We evaluate materiality with reference to all relevant circumstances, including potential market sensitivity.

Cautionary Statement on Forward-Looking Information

 

 

Certain information contained or incorporated by reference in this MD&A, including any information as to our strategy, projects, plans or future financial or operating performance, constitutes “forward-looking statements”. All statements, other than statements of historical fact, are forward-looking statements. anticipated production growth from Barrick’s organic project pipeline and reserve replacement; estimates of future cost of sales per ounce for gold and per pound for copper, total cash costs per ounce and C1 cash costs per pound, and all-in sustaining costs per ounce/pound; cash flow forecasts; projected capital, operating and exploration expenditures; the share buyback program and dividend policy; mine life and production rates; our plans, timelines, and expected completion and benefits of our growth projects, including the Goldrush Project, Fourmile, Ren, Pueblo Viejo plant expansion and mine life extension project, the Nevada Gold Mines Autonomous Haulage Program, Barrick’s Andean portfolio, Veladero Phase 8 Leach Pad, Reko Diq, the Lumwana Super Pit Expansion and the Zaldívar Water Project; anticipated production at Goldrush, Ren, and Lumwana; timing for first production and 2026 and 2027 estimated spend profile on the Lumwana Super Pit Expansion project; Barrick’s decision to slow development activity and reduce capital expenditures at Reko Diq; the ongoing project review of Reko Diq; the development and operation of the Reko Diq project, including project scope, anticipated costs, and timeline for construction and first production; potential significant increases to previously disclosed total estimated capital budget and timeline for the Reko Diq project; capital expenditures related to upgrades and ongoing management initiatives; Barrick’s global exploration strategy and planned exploration activities; Barrick’s copper strategy; the continued ramp up of operations at Loulo-Gounkoto following the resolution of disputes with the Government of Mali, including adoption of the 2023 Mining Code; our pipeline of high confidence projects at or near existing operations; the potential for existing assets to attain Tier One status, including Fourmile; potential mineralization and metal or mineral recoveries; Barrick’s intention to pursue and the expected timing for an initial public offering (“IPO”) of Barrick’s North American gold assets; our ability to convert resources into reserves and future reserve replacement; asset sales, joint ventures and partnerships; Barrick’s strategy, plans, targets and goals in respect of sustainability issues, including climate change, greenhouse gas (“GHG”) emissions reduction targets, safety performance, community development and resettlement, and responsible water use; and expectations regarding future price assumptions, financial performance and other outlook or guidance.

Company as at the date of this MD&A in light of management’s experience and perception of current conditions and expected developments, are inherently subject to significant business, economic and competitive uncertainties and contingencies. Such factors include, but are not limited to: fluctuations in the spot and forward price of gold, copper or certain other commodities (such as silver, diesel fuel, natural gas and electricity); risks associated with projects in the early stages of evaluation and for which additional engineering and other analysis is required; risks related to the possibility that future exploration results will not be consistent with the Company’s expectations, that quantities or grades of reserves will be diminished, and that resources may not be converted to reserves; the speculative nature of mineral exploration and development; lack of certainty with respect to foreign legal systems, corruption and other factors that are inconsistent with the rule of law; changes in national and local government legislation, taxation, controls or regulations and/or changes in the administration of laws, policies and practices, including the expropriation or nationalization of property and political or economic developments in Canada, the United States, or other countries in which Barrick does or may carry on business in the future; Changes in Presentation of Non-GAAP Financial Measures

Attributable Adjusted EBITDA and Attributable Adjusted EBITDA Margin

Starting with our Q2 2026 MD&A, we have renamed attributable EBITDA and attributable EBITDA margin to attributable adjusted EBITDA and attributable adjusted EBITDA margin, respectively. There is no change in the way these measures are calculated.

Attributable Operating Cash Flow

Starting with our Q1 2026 MD&A, we are presenting attributable operating cash flow. Attributable operating cash flow starts with cash provided by operating activities and adds our attributable share of cash provided by operating activities from our equity investees and subtracts the cash provided by operating activities attributable to the non-controlling interests. Management believes this to be a useful indicator of the amount of cash provided by operating activities to Barrick’s ownership share.

Key Business Developments

Nevada Gold Mines

On August 10, 2026, Barrick entered into an agreement with Newmont to expand the assets in the Nevada Gold Mines Joint Venture by agreeing to vend-in their excluded properties: Fourmile from Barrick; Mike and Fiberline from Newmont. Newmont will pay Barrick a top-up payment of $1.95 billion in cash. The agreement resolves all outstanding disputes related to NGM and includes revisions to the NGM joint venture agreement. The agreement also secures Newmont’s consent to Barrick’s proposed North American IPO of its North American gold assets. The members’ interests in NGM will remain unchanged at 61.5% for Barrick and 38.5% for Newmont. We expect the contributions to occur in Q4 2026.

North American Barrick IPO

In April 2026, Barrick announced several executive appointments, dedicated exclusively to our North American gold assets. These assets are comprised of four Tier One Gold Assets5 located in premier mining jurisdictions in North America: Carlin, Cortez, and Turquoise Ridge in the NGM complex, and the Pueblo Viejo mine in the Dominican Republic. North American Barrick will also include the Fourmile, Mike and Fiberline gold projects, located adjacent to NGM, which are expected to be contributed to NGM in Q4 2026, as discussed above.

North American Barrick is expected to be listed on the New York Stock Exchange, subject to satisfaction of customary listing conditions and SEC registration processes. Mark Hill will be the CEO of North American Barrick. Barrick plans to file a S-1 registration statement with respect to the IPO in November, and expects to complete the IPO in the fourth quarter of 2026 or early 2027, subject to market and other conditions and necessary approvals.

New Share Buyback Program

At the May 8, 2026 meeting, the Board of Directors authorized a new share buyback program for the purchase of up to $3 billion of Barrick’s outstanding common shares over the next 12 months. Barrick repurchased $761 million of shares in Q3 2026, following repurchases of $1.209 billion in Q2 2026, bringing the YTD 2026 to $1.970 billion purchased under this share buyback program.

The actual number of common shares that may be purchased, and the timing of any such purchases, will be determined by Barrick based on a number of factors, including the Company’s financial performance, the availability of cash flows, and the consideration of other uses of cash, including capital investment opportunities, returns to shareholders, and debt reduction.

The repurchase program does not obligate the Company to acquire any particular number of common shares, and the repurchase program may be suspended or discontinued at any time at the Company’s discretion.

Executive Leadership Changes

On February 4, 2026, Mark Hill was appointed as President and Chief Executive Officer, following his appointment as Group Chief Operating Officer and Interim President and Chief Executive Officer on September 29, 2025.

Mr. Hill, who was previously responsible for Barrick’s LATAM & Asia Pacific region, is a seasoned mining executive with 30 years of experience. He joined Barrick in 2006 and has experience in strategy, corporate development and leading major projects across the world,

and was also integral in the initial decision to undertake exploration at the Fourmile gold project in Nevada.

On August 11, 2026, Sebastian Bock was appointed as Chief Executive Officer, Rest of World, reporting to Mark Hill. This portfolio combines Barrick’s AME and South America & Asia Pacific regions, and will now be referred to as Barrick International. He joined Barrick in January 2019 as SVP and CFO, Africa and Middle East, and was appointed COO for the region in July 2022.

On March 1, 2026, Helen Cai was appointed as Senior Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer, following the departure of Graham Shuttleworth. Ms. Cai has served on the Barrick Board of Directors since November 2021 and brings more than two decades of experience in equity research, corporate finance, strategic planning, capital markets, and M&A across the mining, industrial, and technology sectors, primarily with Goldman Sachs and China International Capital Corporation.

On February 24, 2026, we announced the appointments of James J. McGuire as Chief Legal and Policy Officer and Woo Lee as Chief Global Affairs Officer. Both Mr. McGuire and Mr. Lee report to Barrick’s President and Chief Executive Officer, Mark Hill, and are now members of the Executive Committee.

Mr. McGuire brings over 30 years of legal (civil and criminal) experience representing leading corporations, financial institutions, and individuals on a wide range of complex legal and policy matters. Effective June 1, 2026, Mr. McGuire became the Chief Legal, Compliance and Policy Officer, and oversees Barrick’s legal, compliance, regulatory, and public policy functions. Poupak Bahamin (most recently Barrick’s General Counsel and Chief Compliance Officer) departed Barrick on June 5, 2026.

Mr. Lee has worked at Barrick for over 11 years, most recently as Senior Vice President and Head of Government & Corporate Affairs, Asia Pacific, where he worked with government officials, business and community leaders to advance the Company’s strategic objectives. As Chief Global Affairs Officer, Mr. Lee leads Barrick’s global government affairs strategy in all markets as well as manages government and sovereign relationships.

On August 7, 2026, Barrick appointed Sarah Ball Teslik as Chief Corporate Affairs Officer and Daniel Wilner as Senior Vice President, Corporate Affairs and Capital Markets, both reporting to Mark Hill, President and Chief Executive Officer. Ms. Teslik joined Barrick from Greenspoon Marder LLP, where she was a Partner and President of its affiliate, Value(s) Management and Investing, and previously served as a Partner at Joele Frank and Senior Vice President at Apache Corporation. Mr. Wilner previously founded and led Stone Pine, a strategic advisory firm serving clients across mining and critical minerals, finance, climate technology, fintech and media, where he advised boards and senior executives on strategy, proxy communications, ESG disclosure, and institutional investor relations.

On September 14, 2026, Barrick made additional changes to the leadership structure. Grant Beringer, Group Sustainability Executive, departed Barrick on September 1, 2026. Ms. Teslik now leads ESG, Governance and Sustainability and Mr. Wilner was appointed Senior Vice President, Chief Communications Officer. Both Ms. Teslik and Mr. Wilner report to Barrick’s President and Chief

At the February 4, 2026 meeting, Robert Samek was appointed to the Board of Directors and has joined the Audit & Risk and Compensation Committees. In addition, Mark Hill, President and Chief Executive Officer, has joined the Company’s Board of Directors as a Non-Independent Director.

Reko Diq

Following the preliminary findings of the review initiated in February 2026 and the further escalation of security issues in the region, on April 2, 2026, the Company announced that it considers it necessary to slow development activity and extend the project review. The continued review will allow the Company to assess in a comprehensive manner the evolving security situation, capital requirements, project financing, project scope and timeline.

Sustainability

Sustainability, including our license to operate, is entrenched in our DNA: our sustainability strategy is our business plan. Please refer to page 17 of our 2025 Annual Report and our 2025 Sustainability Report for a full description of governance, strategy, risk management and targets. Key updates for 2026 are summarized below:

Safety remains our priority. During Q3 2026, the group recorded no fatalities. The TRIFR3 improved quarter on quarter from 0.77 to 0.71, reflecting positive progress in reducing the overall rate of recordable injuries across the group. However, eight LTIs were recorded across the group during the quarter, with the majority being classified as not high potential. The LTIFR3 increased slightly quarter over quarter from 0.15 to 0.19, underscoring the need for continued focus on critical risks and the effectiveness of controls to prevent these outcomes. Prevention of fatalities and life-changing injuries requires sustained focus on critical risks and the effectiveness of critical controls.

Leadership engagement in the field remains strong, with managers and superintendents actively completing CCVs. During Q3 2026, over 24,000 CCVs were completed, with 25% identifying at-risk conditions. Importantly, 79% of these at-risk conditions were resolved in the field, demonstrating effective intervention at the point of risk and reinforcing the desired focus on eliminating hazards before they lead to serious incidents. Improvements in the quality of these activities is a focus and we are making progress in this regard.

During Q3 2026, the Group’s total Scope 1 and 2 (location-based) GHG emissions were 1,848 kt CO2. YTD absolute emissions are trending 5% lower than 2025 due to the divestments of Hemlo and Tongon, and lower emissions from the Goldstrike Roaster and TS Power Plant, partially offset by the restart of Loulo-Gounkoto.

Full Year 2026 Outlook

We continue to expect our 2026 gold production to be in the range of 2.90 to 3.25 million ounces with Q4 2026 expected to be slightly higher than Q3 2026. Gold production for the 9 months YTD continues to be closely aligned with the plan aside from disruptions related to severe weather events at Veladero and Porgera and local grid power instability which has impacted underground performance at North Mara. Consequently, all three sites are expected to be around or below the low end of their respective production guidance ranges.

Our 2026 gold cost guidance remains unchanged noting the ranges in the table to the right are based on a gold price assumption of $4,500/oz which compares to the YTD average realized gold price1 of $4,486/oz. We have previously disclosed that our cost sensitivity is $5/oz for every $100/oz change in the gold price. Higher diesel prices continue to impact our operating costs in particular at our open pit operations, although we have been able to partially offset some of that cost pressure through productivity improvements.

We continue to expect 2026 copper production to be in the range of 190 to 220 thousand tonnes. We also expect that our copper cost guidance metrics for 2026 will be at or slightly above the top end of the ranges given the impact of higher diesel prices and local currency appreciation. Our copper cost guidance provided in February was based on a WTI oil price assumption of $70/bbl and an LME copper price assumption of $5.50/lb which compares to the YTD market average WTI oil price of $86/bbl and realized copper price1 of $6.17/lb. We have previously disclosed that our cost sensitivity is $0.01/lb per $0.25/lb change in the copper price.

In terms of the sensitivity of our costs to the oil price assumptions, we have calculated that for every $10/ barrel change in these oil prices, the direct impact on our costs associated with our diesel consumption is $12/oz across our gold operations and $0.04/lb across our copper sites.

We previously disclosed that our guidance for 2026 total attributable capital expenditure was reduced to $3.8 to $4.2 billion, reflecting a lower current year spend of $450-500 million (50% basis) for the Reko Diq project. This change is reflected in the table to the right and also includes the consequential impact on the copper capital expenditure ranges for 2026. Note that the timing and quantum of capital expenditures for the Reko Diq project remains under review as part of the overall project review.

Financial Results

Q3 2026 compared to Q2 2026

Gold production in Q3 2026 was 2% lower than Q2 2026 mainly driven by lower underground grades mined and processed with the increased focus on underground development, although this was largely offset by record

tonnes processed at the Gold Quarry roaster following the planned Q2 shutdown.

COS/oz2 and TCC/oz1 in Q3 2026 were both 2% lower than Q2 2026, primarily reflecting lower processing costs following the Gold Quarry shutdown in Q2 2026 although this was offset by lower grades processed. In Q3 2026, AISC/oz1 was 2% higher than Q2 2026, due to higher sustaining capital expenditures1, partially offset by the lower TCC/oz1.

Capital expenditures increased by 9% compared to Q2 2026, mainly driven by higher minesite sustaining capital expenditures1 due to increased underground development, and higher project capital expenditures1 driven by increased expenditures on the open pit autonomous haulage project.

Q3 2026 compared to Q3 2025

Gold production for Q3 2026 was 2% higher than Q3 2025, primarily due to the improved processing performance at the Goldstrike autoclave, in addition to record tonnes at the Gold Quarry roaster benefiting both Carlin and Cortez. This was largely offset by lower grades processed related to the re-entry into the Gold Quarry open pit and the focus on underground development.

COS/oz2 and TCC/oz1 for Q3 2026 were 22% and 14% higher, respectively, than Q3 2025, as a result of the lower grades processed and higher diesel prices, in addition to higher royalties driven by the higher realized gold price1. For Q3 2026, AISC/oz1 was 22% higher than Q3 2025 owing to higher TCC/oz1 combined with higher minesite sustaining capital expenditures1.

Capital expenditures were 46% higher than Q3 2025, mainly due to higher minesite sustaining capital expenditures1 driven by increased open pit waste stripping at the Gold Quarry open pit, following the completion of mining at Arturo in Q1 2026, and higher capitalized drilling. Project capital expenditures1 also increased with the continuation of the Ren project and the open pit autonomous haulage project.

YTD 2026 compared to YTD 2025

Gold production for YTD 2026 was 7% higher than YTD 2025, mainly due to higher throughput and improved recoveries at the Goldstrike autoclave, together with higher roaster throughput. This was partially offset by lower grades processed, with the 25% decrease in average processing grade mainly reflecting: changes in the feed mix; a significant increase in low grade heap leach tonnes placed from the Gold Quarry open pit; a 43% increase in autoclave throughput of lower grade material; together with lower underground grades mined. Higher grades processed in the first three months of the year were driven by the Arturo open pit, where mining was completed in Q1 2026, whereas there was mainly waste stripping in Q1 2025. Underground grades mined were also lower for YTD 2026.

COS/oz2 for YTD 2026 was 14% higher than YTD 2025, mainly reflecting higher depreciation associated with the Arturo open pit. TCC/oz1 for YTD 2026 was 3% higher than YTD 2025, primarily driven by higher diesel prices, tariffs and higher royalties due to the higher realized gold price1. For YTD 2026, AISC/oz1 was 2% lower than YTD 2025 driven by lower minesite sustaining capital expenditures1, partially offset by higher TCC/oz1.

Capital expenditures were in line with YTD 2025 as lower minesite sustaining capital expenditures1 were largely offset by higher project capital expenditures1. The lower minesite sustaining capital expenditures1 were primarily due to the final payment on the Komatsu-930 truck fleet occurring in Q1 2025, whereas higher project capital expenditures1 relate to the continuation of the Ren project, the open pit autonomous haulage project, and the additional investment in growth exploration drilling.

Q3 2026 compared to Q2 2026

Gold production in Q3 2026 was 20% higher than Q2 2026, primarily driven by higher grade open pit ore mined and processed through both the oxide mill and the Gold Quarry roaster, with the latter achieving record throughput as

mining advanced into the higher grade zones of the Crossroads pit, consistent with the planned mining sequence. This was partially offset by lower heap leach production, reflecting the timing of ounces placed, with significant tonnes placed in the first half of 2026.

COS/oz2 and TCC/oz1 in Q3 2026 were 8% and 14% lower, respectively, than Q2 2026, primarily driven by the higher grades processed, partially offset by higher royalties applicable to the Crossroads ore. In Q3 2026, AISC/oz1 was 12% lower than Q2 2026, driven by lower TCC/oz1, partially offset by slightly higher minesite sustaining capital expenditures1.

Capital expenditures in Q3 2026 were 4% higher than Q2 2026, due to higher minesite sustaining capital

Q3 2026 compared to Q3 2025

Gold production for Q3 2026 was in line with Q3 2025, as higher grade open pit ore from Crossroads processed through the oxide mill at higher recoveries was offset by lower roaster production, driven by lower underground grades mined and processed at the Carlin roasters, in line with the mine sequence.

COS/oz2 and TCC/oz1 for Q3 2026 were 30% and 19% higher, respectively, than Q3 2025, reflecting higher royalties due to the higher realized gold price1 and increased production from higher royalty areas, higher underground mining costs including ground support, contractor and maintenance costs as Goldrush continues to ramp up, higher diesel prices and the impact of higher tariffs. For Q3 2026, AISC/oz1 was 26% higher than Q3 2025 driven by higher TCC/oz1 and higher minesite sustaining capital expenditures1.

Capital expenditures in Q3 2026 were 38% higher than Q3 2025, primarily due to the timing of equipment deliveries and higher minesite sustaining capital expenditures¹ driven by higher capitalized waste stripping, as the prior year quarter benefited from the completion of waste stripping at Crossroads Phase 6, combined with higher project capital expenditures¹ related to the continued ramp-up at Goldrush and the open pit autonomous haulage project.

YTD 2026 compared to YTD 2025

Gold production for YTD 2026 was 2% lower than YTD 2025, primarily driven by open pit mine sequencing with processing of lower grade ore from Crossroads, whereas in the prior year period higher grade ore was processed from Cortez Pits phase 1. This was partially offset by the ongoing ramp-up at Goldrush. Overall, this resulted in lower grade ore processed at the oxide mill, lower refractory production, and an increase in tonnes placed on the leach pad.

COS/oz2 and TCC/oz1 for YTD 2026 were 34% and 27% higher, respectively, than YTD 2025, reflecting lower grades processed, higher royalties due to both the higher realized gold price1 and increased production from higher royalty areas, higher diesel prices, and the impact of higher tariffs. For YTD 2026, AISC/oz1 increased by 22% compared to YTD 2025, due to higher TCC/oz1 and higher minesite sustaining capital expenditures1 on a per ounce basis.

Capital expenditures for YTD 2026 were 15% higher than YTD 2025, due to an increase in project capital expenditures1 driven by the ongoing ramp-up at Goldrush, the open pit autonomous haulage project and accelerated development at KB South, whereas minesite sustaining capital expenditures1 were almost in line.

Financial Results

Q3 2026 compared to Q2 2026

Gold production in Q3 2026 was in line with Q2 2026, as higher throughput at the Sage autoclave following the planned shutdown in Q2 2026 was offset by lower underground grades mined and processed. Turquoise Ridge Underground delivered record quarterly tonnes mined, with the road header commissioned during the quarter and now ramping up. The road header project

provides additional mining work fronts derisking future ore supply with the potential to increase future tonne delivery.

COS/oz2 and TCC/oz1 in Q3 2026 were 1% lower and in line, respectively, than Q2 2026, primarily driven by lower processing costs following the planned Sage autoclave shutdown in Q2 2026 largely offset by the lower grades processed. AISC/oz1 was 2% higher than Q2 2026, driven by increased minesite sustaining capital expenditures1.

Capital expenditures were 21% higher than Q2 2026, driven by higher minesite sustaining capital expenditures1 due to higher capitalized drilling and the timing of underground mobile equipment deliveries, combined with higher project capital expenditures1 related to the open pit expansion.

Q3 2026 compared to Q3 2025

Gold production for Q3 2026 was 6% lower than Q3 2025, due to lower underground grades mined and processed, as the prior year quarter benefited from mining in a high grade zone of the Turquoise Ridge underground. This was partially offset by higher underground tonnes mined and higher throughput at the Sage autoclave.

COS/oz2 and TCC/oz1 for Q3 2026 were 13% and 21% higher than Q3 2025, primarily owing to lower grades processed, combined with the impact of higher tariffs. AISC/ oz1 was 27% higher than Q3 2025, reflecting higher TCC/ oz1 and higher minesite sustaining capital expenditures1.

Capital expenditures were 107% higher than Q3 2025 driven by higher minesite sustaining capital expenditures1, primarily reflecting higher underground development, as well as higher project capital expenditures1 to expand open pit operations.

YTD 2026 compared to YTD 2025

Gold production for YTD 2026 was 7% higher compared to YTD 2025, primarily due to higher tonnes processed at the Sage autoclave, combined with higher mining rates at Turquoise Ridge underground, increasing the average grade processed.

COS/oz2 and TCC/oz1 for YTD 2026 were 4% and 2% lower, respectively, due to higher productivities and higher average grades processed compared to YTD 2025, partially offset by the impact of higher tariffs. AISC/oz1 was in line with YTD 2025, driven by higher minesite sustaining capital expenditures1, partially offset by lower TCC/oz1.

Capital expenditures for YTD 2026 were 59% higher than YTD 2025, driven by higher minesite sustaining capital expenditures1 and higher project capital expenditures1 to expand open pit operations.

Financial Results

Q3 2026 compared to Q2 2026

Gold production in Q3 2026 decreased 13% over Q2 2026, mainly due to lower autoclave throughput which was impacted by maintenance in the milling circuit, partially offset by higher grades processed resulting from a higher proportion of fresh ore material in the feed.

COS/oz2 and TCC/oz1 for Q3 2026 were both 1% lower than Q2 2026, as a result of higher grades processed and lower royalties due to a lower realized gold price1, partially offset by lower costs allocated to by-products. For Q3 2026, AISC/oz1 was 12% higher than Q2 2026, driven primarily by higher minesite sustaining capital expenditures1.

Capital expenditures for Q3 2026 increased by 24% compared to Q2 2026, driven by higher minesite sustaining capital expenditures1 related to the El Llagal TSF.

Q3 2026 compared to Q3 2025

Gold production for Q3 2026 was 9% lower than Q3 2025, driven by lower throughput combined with lower grades processed in line with the mine and stockpile feed sequence.

COS/oz2 and TCC/oz1 for Q3 2026 were 15% and 8% higher, respectively, compared to Q3 2025, primarily reflecting lower grades processed and higher royalties driven by the increase in the realized gold price1. For Q3 2026, AISC/oz1 was 24% higher than Q3 2025, driven by higher TCC/oz1 and higher minesite sustaining capital expenditures1.

Capital expenditures for Q3 2026 increased by 64% compared to Q3 2025, primarily due to increased minesite sustaining capital expenditures1 relating to the construction of the El Llagal TSF, combined with higher project capital expenditures¹ related to the Naranjo TSF.

YTD 2026 compared to YTD 2025

Gold production for YTD 2026 was 5% higher than YTD 2025, reflecting an increase in autoclave tonnes processed, partially offset by lower grades processed and lower recovery.

COS/oz2 for YTD 2026 was 2% higher than YTD 2025, primarily reflecting higher royalties driven by the higher realized gold price1 and the lower grades processed. TCC/oz1 was 6% lower than YTD 2025, primarily reflecting

Financial Results

Q3 2026 compared to Q2 2026

Gold production for Q3 2026 was 16% higher than Q2 2026, driven by increased throughput and higher grades processed. The operational ramp-up remains ahead of schedule, supported by the mining and processing performance exceeding the restart plan.

COS/oz2, TCC/oz1 and AISC/oz1 for Q3 2026 were almost in line with Q2 2026. The benefit from higher grades processed was offset by the impact of increased mining and processing activity in addition to cost pressures on key consumables.

Q3 2026 compared to Q3 2025

There was no gold production in Q3 2025 due to the suspension of operations midway through January 2025 as a result of the dispute with the Government of Mali that was ultimately resolved in December 2025. This resulted in no gold sales in Q3 2025 and, consequently, no TCC/oz1, AISC/oz1 and COS/oz2 were reported for the period.

YTD 2026 compared to YTD 2025

Gold production for YTD 2025 was also impacted by the suspension of operations discussed above. This resulted in no gold sales in YTD 2025 and consequently, no TCC/oz1, AISC/oz1 and COS/oz2 were reported for the period.

Capital expenditures for YTD 2026 relates to the resumption of operations and spend on critical capital items such as mobile mining equipment and underground development expenditure.

Financial Results

Q3 2026 compared to Q2 2026

Gold production for Q3 2026 was 20% higher than Q2 2026, reflecting improved mine to mill operational performance and higher grades processed. Higher underground mining rates delivered 18% more ore at a 10% higher grade compared to Q2 2026, materially increasing the average grade fed to the processing plant. Open pit mining volumes also increased, providing operational flexibility through stockpile management and supporting a sustained increase in throughput.

COS/oz2 and TCC/oz1 for Q3 2026 were 17% and 20% lower, respectively, primarily reflecting higher grades processed, increased recovery and lower royalty costs due to a lower realized gold price1. For Q3 2026, AISC/oz1 was 16% lower than in Q2 2026, primarily reflecting the lower

TCC/oz1 partially offset by higher minesite sustaining capital expenditures1.

Capital expenditures for Q3 2026 were 8% higher than Q2 2026, driven by higher minesite sustaining capital expenditures1 partially offset by marginally lower project capital expenditures1. The higher minesite sustaining capital expenditures1 were associated with increased capitalized stripping activity in the open pits.

Q3 2026 compared to Q3 2025

Gold production for Q3 2026 was 6% higher than Q3 2025, driven by higher grades processed, resulting from an improved blended feed grade and increased recovery. The stronger blended grade was supported by the strong performance from the underground, which delivered 16% more ore tonnes and enhanced operational flexibility.

COS/oz2 and TCC/oz1 for Q3 2026 were 5% and 8% higher, respectively, compared to Q3 2025, driven by increased labour costs and diesel prices, driving higher unit costs coupled with higher royalties resulting from a higher realized gold price1. For Q3 2026, AISC/oz1 was 11% higher than Q3 2025, driven by higher TCC/oz1 and increased minesite sustaining capital expenditures1.

Capital expenditures for Q3 2026 were 67% higher than Q3 2025, driven by higher minesite sustaining capital

YTD 2026 compared to YTD 2025

Gold production for YTD 2026 was in line with YTD 2025, with higher feed grade and recovery compensating for the slightly lower throughput.

COS/oz2 and TCC/oz1 for YTD 2026 were 12% and 16% higher, respectively, than YTD 2025. The increase was driven by higher labour costs and diesel prices, and increased royalty costs resulting from a higher realized gold price1.

For YTD 2026, AISC/oz1 was 18% higher compared to YTD 2025, mainly due to the higher TCC/oz1, and higher minesite sustaining capital expenditures1.

Capital expenditures in YTD 2026 were 61% higher than YTD 2025, mainly due to an increase in project capital expenditures1 related to the construction of the Pamao TSF project and the development of new underground mining areas, as well as increased minesite sustaining capital expenditures1 resulting from increased capitalized waste stripping costs as we move more waste to unlock the ore from the open pits.

Financial Results

Q3 2026 compared to Q2 2026

In Q3 2026, the focus at North Mara was on open pit mining activity centered around waste material movement in the Gokona pit while addressing delayed delivery of ore from the underground operations. Gold production in Q3 2026 was 6% higher than Q2 2026, mainly driven by an increase in grades processed through the plant, together with higher open pit tonnes.

COS/oz2 and TCC/oz1 for Q3 2026 were 3% and 4% higher, respectively, compared to Q2 2026, mainly due to the impact of additional contractor costs supporting the increased open pit activity. AISC/oz1 in Q3 2026 was 15% higher than Q2 2026, mainly due to higher TCC/oz1 and higher minesite sustaining capital expenditures1.

Capital expenditures for Q3 2026 were 15% lower compared to Q2 2026 mainly driven by lower project capital

expenditures1 related to Gokona pre-stripping activities coming to an end. This was partially offset by higher waste stripping, which was driven by higher unit costs, and higher underground development costs resulting from increased development meters.

Q3 2026 compared to Q3 2025

Gold production for Q3 2026 was 42% lower compared to Q3 2025 mainly due to lower grades processed, lower throughput and lower recoveries, together with a plant shutdown which was used to execute on planned and unplanned maintenance. Grade was impacted by underground sequencing, while lower throughput was driven by local grid instability. We are mitigating the grid instability through multiple projects, including STATCOM installation which is expected to be completed mid next year.

COS/oz2 and TCC/oz1 for Q3 2026 were 89% and 111% higher, respectively, compared to Q3 2025, mainly due to the lower grades processed, combined with higher diesel prices and higher royalties associated with the higher realized gold price1. AISC/oz1 in Q3 2026 was 134% higher than Q3 2025, mainly due to the higher TCC/oz1 and higher minesite sustaining capital expenditures1 than Q3 2025.

For Q3 2026, capital expenditures increased by 10% compared to Q3 2025, mainly due to higher capitalized waste stripping and higher underground development.

YTD 2026 compared to YTD 2025

For YTD 2026, gold production was 46% lower than YTD 2025, as a result of a reduction in underground volumes and grade delivered. The decline in underground performance was primarily driven by grid power instability, which also impacted runtime of the plant. In Q4 2026, we expect to increase mining of higher-grade open pit material. As explained above, projects are underway to address the power instability.

COS/oz2 and TCC/oz1 for YTD 2026 were 88% and 98% higher, respectively, than YTD 2025, mainly driven by the impact of lower grades processed, combined with higher diesel prices and higher royalties associated with the higher realized gold price1. AISC/oz1 for YTD 2026 was 99% higher than YTD 2025, reflecting the increase in TCC/oz1, combined with higher minesite sustaining capital expenditures1 on a per ounce basis.

For YTD 2026, capital expenditures increased by 20% compared to YTD 2025, mainly driven by higher project capital expenditures1 reflecting the ramp-up of the Gokona open pit and second crushing line.

Financial Results

Q3 2026 compared to Q2 2026

Q3 2026 production was 7% higher than Q2 2026 driven by higher grades processed and increased throughput. The Upper West development continues to advance well and has brought flexibility to the mining operations.

COS/oz2 and TCC/oz1 in Q3 2026 were 6% and 5% lower than Q2 2026, respectively, due to the impact of the higher grades processed and lower unit costs in the underground. AISC/oz1 in Q3 2026 was 4% higher than Q2 2026, primarily due to higher minesite sustaining capital expenditures1 related to a catch up post mining commission approval of key sustaining projects partially offset by the lower TCC/oz1.

Capital expenditures in Q3 2026 were 5% higher compared to Q2 2026, reflecting higher minesite sustaining capital expenditures1 driven by the timing of spend on key projects.

Q3 2026 compared to Q3 2025

For Q3 2026, gold production was 24% higher than Q3 2025 mainly driven by higher grades processed and due to strong mining performance in the form of higher volumes, development and grade.

COS/oz2 and TCC/oz1 for Q3 2026 were 4% and 11% lower, respectively, compared to Q3 2025, due to the higher grades processed, partially offset by higher royalties associated with the higher realized gold price1. AISC/oz1 in Q3 2026 was 1% higher than Q3 2025, due to higher sustaining capital spend on a per ounce basis offset by lower TCC/oz1.

For Q3 2026, capital expenditures were 41% higher than Q3 2025, mainly due to higher minesite sustaining capital expenditures1 related to timing of spend on key projects.

YTD 2026 compared to YTD 2025

For YTD 2026, gold production was 10% higher than YTD 2025, due to higher grades processed, partially offset by lower throughput.

COS/oz2 and TCC/oz1 in YTD 2026 were 6% and 1% higher, respectively, than YTD 2025, due to higher royalties associated with the higher realized gold price1 partially offset by higher grades processed. AISC/oz1 for YTD 2026 was 1% lower than YTD 2025, mainly due to lower minesite sustaining capital expenditures on a per ounce basis, partially offset by higher TCC/oz1.

For YTD 2026, capital expenditures increased by 20% compared to YTD 2025, mainly due to higher project capital expenditures1 related to the Upper West project.

Phoenix (61.5%), Nevada, USA

Veladero (50%), Argentina

Gold production for Veladero in Q3 2026 was 25% lower compared to Q2 2026 driven by lower throughput and fewer recoverable ounces placed on the leach pad, as severe winter storms resulted in the temporary suspension of operations on multiple occasions during the quarter. COS/ oz2 and TCC/oz1 in Q3 2026 were 24% and 26% higher, respectively, mainly driven by lower fixed cost dilution as a result of lower sales volume and lower capitalized waste stripping, combined with higher labor costs and road-clearing costs associated with the adverse weather conditions. AISC/oz1 increased by 20% due to higher TCC/ oz1, partially offset by lower minesite sustaining capital expenditures1 due to lower stripping and the timing of expenditure.

Porgera (24.5%), Papua New Guinea

Gold production in Q3 2026 was 35% lower than Q2 2026 driven by lower throughput as water shortages associated with the El Niño weather event reduced processing plant operating rates. This was partially offset by higher grades processed. COS/oz2 was 3% lower than Q2 2026 due to lower depreciation partially offset by higher TCC/oz1. TCC/ oz1 increased by 6% compared to Q2 2026, mainly due to lower fixed cost dilution as a result of lower sales volume together with higher transport and freight costs. AISC/oz1 increased by 20% due to higher TCC/oz1 and higher minesite sustaining capital expenditures1 related to capitalized waste stripping and underground development.

Financial Results

Q3 2026 compared to Q2 2026

Copper production in Q3 2026 was 15% lower than in Q2 2026 mainly due to lower grades processed driven by the rescheduling of the planned mill reline into September which deferred the processing of high grade ore into October.

COS/lb2 and C1 cash costs/lb1 were 11% and 14% higher, respectively, than Q2 2026. This is predominantly due to higher diesel prices which impacted mining costs. In addition, increased maintenance costs were incurred on preventative maintenance to improve fleet availabilities and address premature equipment failures. In Q3 2026, AISC/ lb1 was 20% higher than Q2 2026, driven by the higher C1 cash costs/lb1 mentioned above as well as elevated royalty costs from a higher realized copper price1 in Q3 and higher minesite sustaining capital expenditures1.

Capital expenditures for Q3 2026 were 38% higher than Q2 2026. This was attributable to a higher spend on the Super Pit Expansion project as per the project

execution plan with increased spending on fleet, EPCM costs, SMPP works (wet and dry plant) as well as cabling. Minesite sustaining capital expenditures1 were 26% higher than Q2 2026 driven by higher stripping costs which were attributable to the higher diesel prices as discussed above.

Q3 2026 compared to Q3 2025

Copper production for Q3 2026 was 8% lower than Q3 2025, mainly due to lower grades processed driven by the rescheduling of the planned mill reline into September which deferred the processing of high grade ore into October. This was offset by a higher throughput rate attributable to the improved power stability and the addition of the new pebble crusher.

COS/lb2 and C1 cash costs/lb1 for Q3 2026 increased by 50% and 60%, respectively, compared to Q3 2025, mainly due to the higher diesel prices as well as the local currency appreciation driving higher labour costs. For Q3 2026, AISC/lb1 was 57% higher than Q3 2025 due to increased C1 cash costs/lb1 as well as higher royalties from higher realized copper prices and higher minesite sustaining capital expenditures1.

Capital expenditures for Q3 2026 were 67% higher than Q3 2025, mainly due to increased project capital expenditures1 on the Super Pit Expansion project. Minesite sustaining capital expenditures1 were 41% higher than Q3 2025 mainly driven by higher stripping costs caused by the same C1 cash cost pressures referred to above (diesel and currency appreciation).

Fourmile, Nevada, USA

Fourmile is a 100% Barrick-owned asset in Nevada, located adjacent to Goldrush, that has the potential to be a Tier One Gold Asset5. In Q3 2026 Barrick announced that an agreement had been reached with Newmont to contribute Fourmile into the NGM joint venture. Barrick continues advanced studies to support ongoing resource development with expected completion in 2029.

Drilling activities continued in Q3 2026, and step-out drilling intersected significant intercepts outside of the current resource. Infill and resource definition drilling remained a priority during the quarter to support the ongoing PFS. Drilling will focus on the southern zones ahead of the planned winter drilling program.

The Fourmile studies continued to advance ventilation, mine design, paste backfill, geotechnical, hydrogeology, and metallurgical workstreams throughout Q3 2026.

Early works to support the Bullion Hill Decline are underway, with a ramp up expected in Q4 2026 pending permits. Barminco mobilization is underway in preparation for the start of decline development.

Across drilling, studies, and capital activities, we spent $53 million in Q3 2026 and $123 million year to date. Total spend for 2026 includes an anticipated drilling spend of $150 to $160 million together with ~$15 million of spend on studies work (both expensed) and ~$30 million on construction and decline commencement (capital). This phase of the project has been approved with an estimated total cost of $360 to $430 million extending through mid-2030.

Goldrush Project, Nevada, USA6

Goldrush, which is included within Cortez, is expected to be a long-life underground mine with anticipated annual production in excess of 400,000 ounces of gold per year (100% basis) once in full production by 2028.

In Q3 2026, execution planning continued for key infrastructure projects. Ventilation modeling and optimization for the third surface ventilation shaft was completed in Q2 2026 and geotechnical drilling was completed in Q3 2026 to validate shaft location and provide contractual details for shaft sinking contract negotiations.

Detailed engineering for the underground paste backfill plant progressed and major equipment procurement commenced in Q3 2026. The surface and underground mixing plant locations were finalized and development underground is planned to start early in 2027. Contract negotiations for an EPCM agreement were concluded in Q3 2026.

The portal pad access road widening started and is expected to be completed in Q4 2026 to improve traffic flow and allow for optimized ore hauling to mill staging stockpile pads near Cortez Hills Underground.

Construction of the second surface ventilation shaft progressed slower than scheduled due to lost time associated with a safety incident and stand down although the construction remains on track and is expected to be completed early in Q4 2026. The main underground fans are scheduled to be commissioned in early 2027.

Goldrush completed the underground water filtration system design, finished development of the top level of the system, and plans to mobilize contractors in Q4 2026 to construct sumps and pump foundations for the two-

stage water treatment system. Completion of an additional cement storage silo will support mining operations, while trailers have been secured and will expand existing dry and office buildings, and utility connections (scheduled for Q4 2026).

As of September 30, 2026, project spend was $531 million on a 100% basis (including $14 million in Q3 2026) inclusive of the exploration declines. This capital spent to date, together with the remaining expected pre-production capital, is in line with the approximate $1 billion initial capital estimate for the Goldrush project (100% basis).

Ren, Nevada, USA7

Ren is a new ore deposit at Goldstrike Underground and a key expansion project at Carlin. Located north of Goldstrike Underground’s Meikle and Banshee deposits, Ren is anticipated to produce an average of 140,000 ounces per year (contained ounces, 100% basis) once in full production in 2027.

To develop the deposit, the existing exploration drift has been duplicated, allowing for increased ventilation and secondary egress into the working area. Additional exploration drilling platforms have been constructed from the duplicate drift to support further drilling for both existing resource conversion and further deposit growth. Work has been started on installing paste backfilling infrastructure from Meikle to the new stope locations.

To support production mining of the deposit, an additional set of twin declines will be driven from the Betze-Post West Barrel open pit layback, extending to the north with the intent to provide life of mine ventilation and a direct path for material to be hauled and hoisted out via the existing Meikle Headframe. To complete the project, a ventilation shaft will be sunk 550 meters to serve as an exhaust raise and utility conduit for mining the orebody.

For Q3 2026, resource conversion drilling continued, with approximately 13,300 meters of indicated conversion drilling and 6,400 meters of inventory conversion drilling completed year-to-date. Results continue to support the geological interpretation of discrete mineralized domains across JB North and JB South, with strong intercepts within the existing gold domains. Exploration is increasingly focused on growth opportunities along the Corona corridor and the newly identified Medusa mineralization. Resource modeling is underway, with an updated estimate expected in Q4 2026. Work at the West Barrel declines continued with 735 meters of decline development. The Ren ventilation shaft completed sinking infrastructure commissioning and started ramp up of the main sinking phase, reaching a sinking depth of 215 meters below collar. Production sinking commenced in early Q2 2026 with expected fan commissioning completion and ventilation benefit to be realized in Q3 2027.

As of September 30, 2026, project spend was $246 million (including $28 million in Q3 2026) out of an estimated capital cost of $410 to $470 million (100% basis).

Autonomous Haulage Program, Nevada, USA

The Autonomous Haulage Program is a strategic NGM initiative to improve safety, productivity, and operating consistency. This will be a phased deployment, starting at Cortez and expanding to other NGM operations as fleet, infrastructure, and site readiness milestones are met.

At Cortez, the retrofit of 23 haul trucks was completed in May 2026. The transition to the new Fleet Management System for the primary production fleet has been completed, and the fleet is running in satellite pits for production and training with over 11 million tonnes hauled to date. The transition to the new Fleet Management System is expected to be completed for all Support Equipment in Q4 2026 ahead of the H1 2027 site-wide rollout.

At Carlin, we plan to undertake 40 truck retrofits with the work having commenced in Q2 2026, and 9 of the 40 trucks have been converted to date. Fleet conversion, mine planning, traffic controls, and workforce engagement are advancing with autonomous operations planned to commence in Q1 2027.

At Turquoise Ridge, 20 haul trucks have been ordered as “Autonomous Ready”. Similar to Carlin, fleet conversion, mine planning, traffic controls and workforce engagement have begun. Following delivery, assembly of the first units of the fleet at Turquoise Ridge are expected in Q1 2027. Autonomous operations at the site are expected to commence by mid 2027 and ramp up through the remainder of 2027 as the rest of the fleet is delivered and assembled.

As of September 30, 2026, Cortez had spent $41 million of an approved capital budget of ~$50 million (100% basis). Carlin project expenditures are progressing in line with the planned retrofit schedule, with expected 2026 expenditure of ~$30 million and total program spending through 2027 of ~$65 million (100% basis). Similarly, Turquoise Ridge project expenditures are progressing in line with the planned delivery schedule, with expected 2026 expenditure to be ~$70 million and total program spending through 2027 to be ~$120 million (100% basis).

Pueblo Viejo Expansion, Dominican Republic8

The Pueblo Viejo life of mine expansion continues to advance with resettlement nearing completion and efforts focused on the Naranjo TSF and associated facilities. The TWMS has surpassed 20% completion while Starter Dam detailed design is progressing on schedule to support a full permitting package submission in Q1 2027. Haul Roads 19 and 17 continue to advance, with two of the four bridges now under construction. The remaining self-perform fleet required for Starter Dam construction is also beginning to arrive on site. Construction of the new effluent treatment plant and diorite crusher continues to progress, alongside development of the diorite quarry. In parallel, the site water management PFS has been initiated with Fluor and Piteau, incorporating a new water treatment system aligned with the site long term sustainability plan.

The EPCM contract for the addition of a 4th Lime Kiln has been advanced in Q3 2026 together with the PFS work to improve the flotation circuit with the addition of high shear float cells and upgrades to the existing float cells.

The housing project at Pueblo Viejo continues with our current area of focus being advancing the church and polytechnical school design, along with the agreed 63 government houses. 99% of resettlement packages have now been accepted.

As at September 30, 2026, total project spend was $1,336 million (including $35 million in Q3 2026) on a 100% basis. The estimated capital cost of the plant expansion and mine life extension project remains approximately $2.6 billion (100% basis).

Andean Portfolio9

Barrick continued its early-stage review of development options across its Andean portfolio in Argentina and Chile, which includes the Veladero mine, as well as the El Alto and Lama districts, which encompass the mineralized system historically explored as part of the Pascua-Lama project, and the Norte Abierto project. These deposits (El Alto, Lama and Norte Abierto) represent one of the largest undeveloped gold resource bases in the region, holding more than 42 million ounces of gold in attributable measured and indicated resources as at December 31, 2025, together with approximately 2.3 million tonnes of copper and 788 million ounces of silver, as reported in Barrick’s year-end 2025 mineral reserves and resources statement. The drilling, studies and permitting now underway are intended to define the development pathway that best realizes this opportunity.

At El Alto, in Alto del Carmen, Chile, a two-season drilling campaign is scheduled to commence in Q4 2026 under an approved environmental permit.

At Norte Abierto, a 50/50 joint venture with Newmont in Chile’s Maricunga belt, pre-feasibility studies continued to evaluate the preferred project scope. Studies are expected to progress into 2027 to further define the potential development pathway.

Finally, at Lama, in Argentina, infill drilling and potential deposit extensions have been incorporated into an upcoming campaign to support the advancement of studies and define the scope of work for 2027.

Veladero Phase 8 Leach Pad, Argentina

The construction of the Phase 8 leach pad is being executed in three phases which are named 8A, 8B and 8C. Phases 8A and 8B have been completed on schedule. The phased execution of the project provides flexibility to align future stages with economic conditions and the applicable regulatory framework. Construction of the project includes cutting, filling, sub-drainage and monitoring, leak collection and recirculation, waterproofing, as well as pregnant leaching solution collection.

Overall, the total Phase 8 leach pad project spend at September 30, 2026 was $140 million ($9 million in Q3 2026) out of an estimated capital cost of approximately $250 million (100% basis).

Reko Diq Project, Pakistan10

On February 5, 2026, the Company announced that it was reviewing all aspects of the Reko Diq project in light of the escalation of security risks and increased security incidents. On April 2, 2026, Barrick announced that following the preliminary findings of the review and further escalation of security issues in the region, the Company considers it necessary to slow the development activity and extend the project review. This review is ongoing and will assess in a comprehensive manner the evolving security situation, capital requirements, project financing, project scope and timeline.

Capital expenditures commenced in Q2 2024, with total capitalized spend to date of $1,497 million (including $159 million in Q3 2026) (100% basis).

As previously disclosed, the expected range for 2026 attributable capital expenditure was reduced to $450 to $500 million (50% basis). It is anticipated that there could be significant increases to the previously disclosed total estimated capital budget and timeline for the project. The previously disclosed total estimated capital cost of Phase 1 was between $5.6 billion and $6.0 billion (100% basis, exclusive of capitalization of financing costs) and of Phase

Kibali Solar Project, DRC

This project entailed the design, supply and installation of a 16 MW photovoltaic solar farm with a 15 MW battery energy storage system to complement the existing hydroelectric power stations, increasing the renewable component of the mine’s energy mix. The project was completed in Q1 2026, and the solar photovoltaic power plant generated 22,58 GWh of electrical energy year-to-date, which resulted in estimated year-to-date fuel savings of around 5.65 million liters. The project spend was $46 million, which was below the estimated capital cost of $55 million (100% basis).

Lumwana Super Pit Expansion, Zambia11

The Lumwana Super Pit Expansion is projected to deliver 240,000 tonnes of copper production per annum, from a 52Mtpa process plant expansion, with a mine life of more than 30 years.

The project is on schedule with the target of first copper production at the end of Q1 2028. The critical path for the process plant expansion, the mill building, has been maintained and the final wall lifts are expected to be completed in Q4 2026. The primary crusher construction remains on track with its third level nearing completion and civil construction of the overland conveyors and transfer towers progressing well. The manufacturing and delivery of structural steel are advancing as planned and is sustained by the critical path structural engineering that is expected to be completed in Q4 2026. Procurement of all major long-lead equipment is complete. Deliveries to site continue as per schedule. The third phase of on-site accommodation showed steady progress and continues to support the expansion’s ramp-up. The TSF expansion contract was awarded in Q3 2026 and works are on track to commence in Q4 2026. Road construction supporting the future Kamisengo mining development, where the Kamisengo inflow control dam is being constructed, is on track. Expansion of the mine fleet continues, with the primary mine fleet for 2026 complete. Planned deliveries for next year are well advanced with a PC7000 Komatsu to be commissioned in Q4 2026 and eight Komatsu 930E dump trucks on track for delivery in Q4 2026 with commissioning expected in Q1 2027.

With ongoing progress on the detailed engineering, procurement, and construction, the overall project remains on schedule and is focused on delivery of critical milestones in line with the execution plan. As at September 30, 2026, the total spend on the expansion project was $795 million (including $185 million in Q3 2026 and noting this is inclusive of $38 million spent on the feasibility study completed in 2024). The forecast for 2026 expenditure is now expected to be at the lower end of the $750 to $850 million range. The total project capital cost (exclusive of capitalized stripping) is expected to be $2 billion based on the approved feasibility study.

Zaldívar Water Project, Chile

The Third-Party Water Supply Project, involving the construction of an approximately 160 km pipeline and pumping system to deliver around 200 liters per second of reprocessed wastewater from Antofagasta, has been approved. The project will enable the transition away from continental water sources by mid-2028, as required under

the environmental permit approved in 2025, securing a long-term water supply and supporting a potential extension of the mine life to 2051.

As at September 30, 2026, the total spend on the water project was $145 million (including $72 million in Q3 2026). The estimated capital cost is anticipated to be approximately $950 million (100% basis).

Exploration12, 13

During Q3 2026, Barrick’s exploration teams have been active across all our operations, with strong results returned from drilling across NGM, and at Fourmile, and Kibali in the DRC.

In North America, following the establishment of dedicated greenfield exploration teams for the Great Basin and Western Cordillera, Barrick continued to identify new exploration opportunities and advance its consolidated district-scale land positions during Q3 2026. In the Great Basin, Barrick initiated an extensive geophysical campaign to acquire new datasets over the next 12 months, aiming to improve the understanding of geological and structural controls on mineralization, and support the generation and advancement of new and current exploration targets. During the quarter, gravity surveys were completed at Buckhorn, Goldfield Hills and Patty, with additional surveys progressing across priority areas. Framework drilling advanced at Toiyabe, while permits were secured for initial drilling at other early-stage targets. Regional geological mapping and extensive soil and rock-chip sampling programs also progressed, aimed at identifying and delineating Carlin-type geochemical anomalies and refining the extent of prospective target areas. This work supported additional land consolidation in selected areas. Barrick also executed an earn-in agreement with Greenlight Metals for the Kalium Canyon Project, securing an opportunity to advance a prospective epithermal gold system within the Walker Lane corridor. Collectively, these activities reflect the acceleration of greenfield exploration across the Great Basin, one of Barrick’s key strategic exploration priorities. In the Superior Province, Barrick executed an earn-in agreement with GFG Resources in August covering approximately 475 km2 of consolidated ground along a prospective structural corridor with potential to host greenstone-hosted gold mineralization. Initial geological mapping and sampling are underway, with geophysical surveys planned to support target delineation. Exploration also progressed across other priority districts in the Superior Province through geological mapping and sampling, ground geophysical surveys, till sampling programs and framework drilling. These activities support the systematic advancement of the Superior Province as another key focus area for Barrick’s greenfield exploration strategy.

In Jamaica, exploration continued across three prioritized camp-scale areas targeting epithermal gold and porphyry copper–gold systems. Two drill-ready targets have been defined, with permits secured for the first target and drilling expected to commence during Q4 2026. At Pueblo Viejo in the Dominican Republic, a large-scale induced polarization (IP) geophysical survey was completed to identify concealed chargeability anomalies potentially associated with sulfide mineralization. Results will be integrated with existing geological and geophysical datasets to refine exploration targets and guide follow-up activities. Brownfields exploration at NGM continued across all districts during Q3 2026, with significant drilling results returned from the Carlin and Cortez districts. In the Carlin District, drilling along the approximately two-kilometer-long

Pathfinder corridor, located approximately 500 meters from Goldstrike Underground, intersected high-grade gold mineralization in an area with limited historical drilling. Hole PFX-26011 returned 18.3 meters at 6.45 g/t Au from 347.47 meters, including 1.5 meters at 16.18 g/t Au from 347.47 meters, and 9.1 meters at 12.97 g/t Au from 400.81 meters, while PFX-26005 returned 10.7 meters at 7.80 g/t Au from 522.73 meters. These holes, located more than 500 meters apart, demonstrate the potential for additional high-grade mineralization beyond the existing Goldstrike Underground resource areas. Further north, underground drilling at Ren intersected previously unidentified high-grade mineralization more than 700 meters from existing development. Hole MRC-26034 returned 39.3 meters at 7.32 g/t Au from 740.10 meters, highlighting the potential for further discoveries along the North Carlin Trend. Follow-up surface drilling is planned for Q4 2026. In the Cortez District, deep surface drilling at North Crow, between the Rose and Goldrush orebodies, returned significant high-grade intercepts in a previously underexplored corridor. Hole GRC-26001 intersected 58.7 meters at 24.40 g/t Au from 602.10 meters, 21.6 meters at 35.45 g/t Au from 672.70 meters, and 48.3 meters at 20.14 g/t Au from 707.10 meters. These results confirm the presence of high-grade mineralization between the northern extent of Goldrush and the Rose orebody, supporting the potential for further resource growth in the district. Follow-up drilling is ongoing. At Turquoise Ridge, underground drilling continued at the Dune target to evaluate extensions of the high-grade mineralization identified earlier in 2026.

In South America, early-stage exploration continued in Peru. In the Yauri District, the potential within the district was confirmed by fieldwork with four targets delineated with drill permitting now underway - which is expected to commence in late Q1 2027, after the wet season. In the Tartaro District of northern Peru, land consolidation was completed, securing an 861 km² district-scale position. Early-stage exploration is well advanced, with four target-scale areas of interest identified. One of these areas has been prioritized for target delineation work, while further field validation of the remaining three areas is expected to commence next. In Argentina, within the Veladero District, a further drilling campaign at Porfiada is planned for Q4 2026 to fully define the extent of the known, open mineralization. A detailed safety assessment is underway to confirm appropriate operating conditions following the winter season.

In Africa and the Middle East, field work and drilling continued across the portfolio through the third quarter. In Tanzania, large-scale ground geophysical and drilling programs commenced around North Mara and across Barrick’s expansive and highly prospective greenfield portfolio. Most assay results are still pending, but initial observations are encouraging, with indications of significant deformation, lithological complexity and signs of alteration normally associated with a prospective geological setting. Programs will continue to accelerate through the rest of the field season. Drilling has commenced on the highly prospective copper exploration portfolio in the Copperbelt in DRC, testing a range of large soil anomalies whilst delineation programs advance to define the next phase of targets. At Kibali, the next chapter of growth continued to take shape close to the existing KCD deposit, consistent with the continued ARK growth reported last quarter. The project is rapidly advancing, with conversion and study work well under way, and with drilling continuing to further extend the system of multiple, open, high-grade ore-shoots. As planned, this quarter, drilling began across several high-potential targets in the core KCD corridor to the north-west, south-east and underneath the main

 

mineralized system, and early results indicate significant discovery potential for additional open pit and underground resources. Drilling in the fourth quarter is planned to progress these near-mine targets. In Saudi Arabia, exploration commenced in earnest on the new greenfield North Siham project, located on the extension of the Central Arabian Gold Belt. Early indications are positive, with signs of mineralization in surface samples, and work is progressing to generate targets for more focused follow-up. Meanwhile, near the Jabal Sayid mine, drilling is progressing on the Khamsa target, with a geological model update planned for the fourth quarter to vector toward the parts of the system with the highest potential for a significant satellite deposit.

Q3 2026 compared to Q2 2026

In Q3 2026, gold revenues on a consolidated basis decreased by 4% compared to Q2 2026, driven by a lower realized gold price1, partially offset by higher sales volumes. The average market price for Q3 2026 was $4,262/oz, representing a 5% decrease versus the $4,506/oz average in Q2 2026. During Q3 2026, the gold price ranged from $3,960/oz to $4,697/oz, and closed the quarter at $4,176/ oz. Gold price volatility in Q3 2026 was driven primarily by economic and geopolitical concerns, in particular the ongoing conflict in the Middle East.

  In Q3 2026, gold production on an attributable basis increased by 3% compared to Q2 2026 mainly due to higher grade open pit ore mined and processed at Cortez, improved mine to mill operational performance and higher grades processed at Kibali, and increased throughput and higher grades processed at Loulo-Gounkoto, partially offset by lower throughput at Pueblo Viejo and at Veladero (included within “Other” in the chart above) as severe winter storms resulted in the temporary suspension of operations on multiple occasions during the quarter.

 

ATTRIBUTABLE GOLD PRODUCTION VARIANCE (000s oz)

Q3 2026 compared to Q2 2026

 

In Q3 2026, copper revenues on a consolidated basis decreased by 8% compared to Q2 2026, primarily due to lower sales volumes, partially offset by a higher realized copper price1. The average market price in Q3 2026 was $6.40/lb, representing an all-time high quarterly average and an increase of 6% from the $6.05/lb average in Q2 2026. The realized copper price1 in both Q3 2026 and Q2 2026 was higher than the market copper price due to the timing of sales. During Q3 2026, the copper price traded in a range of $5.94/lb to $6.75/lb, and closed the quarter at $6.57/lb. Copper prices in Q3 2026 were impacted by concerns about the global economy resulting from global trade disputes, supply disruptions, the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, and demand forecasts in China, which is the world’s largest consumer of copper.

  Attributable copper production in Q3 2026 was 6 thousand tonnes lower compared to Q2 2026 driven by a planned shutdown for a mill reline at Lumwana that was brought forward to late September, deferring the processing of high-grade ore to October.

For Q3 2026, gold revenues on a consolidated basis increased by 20% compared to Q3 2025, primarily due to a higher realized gold price1, partially offset by lower sales volumes. The average market price for Q3 2026 was $4,262/oz versus $3,457/oz for Q3 2025.

YTD 2026 compared to YTD 2025

This was partially offset by lower production at North Mara, mainly due to lower grades processed driven by lower grades mined.

Q3 2026 compared to Q2 2026

In Q3 2026, gold cost of sales on a consolidated basis was 1% lower than Q2 2026, primarily due to lower unit costs as described below. Our 45% interest in Kibali and 24.5% interest in Porgera are equity accounted, and therefore each mine’s cost of sales is excluded from our consolidated gold cost of sales. Our per ounce metrics, gold COS/oz2 and TCC/oz1, include our proportionate share of cost of sales at our equity method investees, and were 2% and 3% lower, respectively, compared to Q2 2026 primarily driven by changes in the sales mix across the portfolio, the shutdown activity in Q2 2026 and the impact of lower royalties due to a lower realized gold price1.

  In Q3 2026, gold AISC/oz1, which also includes our proportionate share of equity method investees, was 2% higher than Q2 2026, as higher minesite sustaining capital expenditures1 were partially offset by lower TCC/oz1, as explained above.

  In Q3 2026, copper cost of sales on a consolidated basis was 5% lower than Q2 2026, primarily due to lower sales volumes. Our 50% interests in Zaldívar and Jabal Sayid are equity accounted and therefore, we do not include their cost of sales in our consolidated copper cost of sales. Our per pound metrics, copper COS/lb2 and C1 cash costs/lb1, include our proportionate share of cost of sales at our equity method investees. Copper COS/lb2 and C1 cash costs/lb1 were 8% and 12% higher, respectively, compared to Q2 2026, primarily driven by higher diesel prices and

Q3 2026 compared to Q3 2025

For Q3 2026, gold cost of sales on a consolidated basis was 23% higher than Q3 2025, mainly due to increased site operating costs, higher depreciation and increased royalties driven by the higher realized gold price1. This was partially offset by lower sales volumes. As described above, our per ounce metrics, gold COS/oz2 and TCC/oz1, include our proportionate share of cost of sales at our equity method investees, and were 25% and 22% higher, respectively, compared to Q3 2025. This was mainly due to the impact of higher diesel prices across all operations, higher royalties associated with the higher realized gold price1 (impact approximately $60/oz), the change in the sales mix by site, higher tariffs at the NGM operations and the impacts related to adverse weather conditions at Veladero and Porgera.

  For Q3 2026, gold AISC/oz1 was 24% higher than Q3 2025, primarily due to higher TCC/oz1, combined with higher minesite sustaining capital expenditures1.

  For Q3 2026, copper cost of sales on a consolidated basis was 38% higher than Q3 2025, primarily due to higher site operating costs, partially offset by lower sales volumes. As described above, our per pound metrics, copper COS/lb2 and C1 cash costs/lb1, include our proportionate share of cost of sales at our equity method investees. Copper COS/lb2 and C1 cash costs/lb1 were 36% and 41% higher, respectively, compared to Q3 2025, mainly due to higher diesel prices as well as the local currency appreciation driving up higher labour costs.

  For Q3 2026, copper AISC/lb1 was 44% higher than Q3 2025, mainly due to higher C1 cash costs/lb1, increased royalties due to the higher realized copper price1 and increased minesite sustaining capital expenditures1 primarily at Lumwana.

YTD 2026 compared to YTD 2025

For YTD 2026, gold cost of sales on a consolidated basis was 23% higher than YTD 2025, mainly due to higher site operating costs, increased depreciation, and higher royalties and mining and production taxes associated with the higher realized gold price1. On a per ounce basis, gold COS/oz2 and TCC/oz1, after including our proportionate share of COS at our equity method investees (refer to explanation above), were 21% and 15% higher, respectively, than YTD 2025. This was primarily due to higher diesel prices across all operations, higher royalties (impact approximately $75/oz) associated with the higher realized gold price1, the change in the sales mix by site, lower grades processed at Cortez and North Mara, and higher costs associated with the adverse weather conditions at Veladero and Porgera.

  For YTD 2026, gold AISC/oz1 increased by 10% compared to YTD 2025, primarily due to an increase in TCC/oz1, partially offset by lower minesite sustaining capital expenditures1 on a per ounce basis.

  For YTD 2026, copper cost of sales on a consolidated basis was 29% higher than YTD 2025,

 

primarily due to higher site operating costs and increased royalties associated with the higher realized copper price1, partially offset by lower sales volumes. Our per pound metrics, copper COS/lb2 and C1 cash costs/lb1, include our proportionate share of COS at our equity method investees (refer to explanation above). Copper COS/lb2 and C1 cash costs/lb1 were 28% and 30% higher, respectively, compared to YTD 2025, due to higher diesel prices and local currency appreciation at Lumwana as discussed above.

  For YTD 2026, copper AISC/lb1 was 34% higher than YTD 2025, primarily due to higher C1 cash costs/lb1, as discussed above, as well as higher royalties due to the higher realized copper price1.
